judgment.rationale: First SFI (Grade 2, rank 2, Term 1, Writing / Handwriting): 'Writes and uses punctuation marks (full stops, question marks, commas, exclamation marks)', with LCs for forming punctuation marks and for using them. Second SFI (Grade 1, rank 1, Term 2, Writing / Shared, Group and Independent Writing): 'Writes and illustrates a caption or short sentence on a topic to contribute to a book for the reading corner', with LCs for writing and for illustrating that caption/short sentence. Both sit in the Writing skill area and both concern sentence-level written production, so they form a coherent, mutually reinforcing pair: punctuation marks are the conventions applied to the kind of short sentences learners compose for a class book. This is more than generic repeated wording, so no_relation is not appropriate. However, the evidence does not support a developmental dependency: the Grade 2 bullet introduces punctuation formation and usage, a Handwriting-sub-strand capability wholly absent from the Grade 1 composition bullet, and the only cross-endpoint signals supplied are the generic shared tokens 'writes'/'writing' (sfi jaccard 0.08; lc tag jaccard 0.10), shared Writing skill-area placement, and weak local-rank proximity (rank gap 1) - none of which, alone or together, demonstrate that Grade 1 caption writing is a substantive precursor whose proficiency raises the likelihood of success at punctuating. Symmetric relatesTo therefore retains the genuine coherence without over-claiming direction. Material limitations: both endpoints have 24 omitted source-evidence items (truncated evidence) and all endpoints and ancestors carry upstream audit/merge/code context warnings, which are preserved below and bound the confidence of this judgment.

judgment.rationale: Both are distinct printed bullets in the same Grade 3, Term 1, WRITING, 'Shared, Group and Independent Writing' table (page 113, window 44), with identical coordinate rank (Grade 3) and no term difference to supply developmental order. One targets grammatical accuracy in sentence construction (present, past and future tense used correctly); the other targets sentence formation with a broad range of punctuation (capital letters, full stops, question marks, commas, exclamation marks, inverted commas). These are complementary written-language convention skills that reinforce each other in composing correct sentences, but neither statement's evidence shows that proficiency in tense use supports success with punctuation conventions or vice versa, so no developmental dependency is asserted. Shared LC token overlap is limited to the generic 'writing' tag and the word 'and', which alone would not support a relation; the substantive coherence is the shared sub-strand purpose of accurate independent sentence writing. Both endpoints' source evidence is truncated (24 omitted items each), so absence of further distinguishing text is not proven.

judgment.rationale: Both are Grade R (rank 0) rhyme-focused Skills, but at different terms and skill areas: the second SFI sits in Grade R Term 2, Emergent Reading, Sub-strand 'Phonological/Phonemic Awareness' ('Anticipates rhyming words in new songs and rhymes and completes the line or sentence'), while the first sits in Grade R Term 4, Emergent Writing, Sub-strand 'Works with words' ('Groups pictures of rhyming words such as "can", "fan", "pan"'). The Term 2 skill is oral, supported rhyme recognition within familiar song/rhyme patterns; the Term 4 skill requires the learner to independently detect shared rimes across decontextualised picture sets and categorise them, a substantive extension from predicting a rhyme in context to deliberately sorting rhyme families. Proficiency in anticipating and completing rhymes therefore supports success in grouping rhyming pictures, giving an earlier-Term to later-Term direction within Grade R (second_to_first). Shared LC tag/text tokens ('rhyming', 'words') alone were not treated as sufficient; the judgment rests on the term/sub-strand placement and the increase in independence and task demand. Source evidence for both endpoints is truncated, limiting fuller context, but the printed statements and identity scopes are unambiguous.

judgment.rationale: Both Skills sit in the same Grade 2 (rank 2), Term 3, Reading and Phonics / 'Daily Phonic Activities' sub-strand, so direction cannot rest on grade or term order and must come from content. The second SFI is a specific word-level grapheme-recognition skill (recognising common double consonants ll, ss, zz at word endings, e.g. do-ll, fu-ss, buzz); the first SFI is the application skill of reading words taught in phonics lessons within sentences and other connected texts. Mastery of the specific double-consonant pattern is one of the phonic elements a learner applies when decoding phonics words in running text, so the element-level recognition supports success in the text-level application rather than the reverse. Evidence is limited to shared-parent hierarchy, same source page/table row, and LC tags ('phonics'); token overlap is low (jaccard ~0.08) and both endpoints have truncated source evidence (and the first also truncated LC evidence), so the inference rests on the full statement texts rather than complete source context, hence moderate confidence.

Proficiency in the Term 2 skill therefore supports success in the Term 4 skill, so buildsTowards second_to_first (Term 2 to Term 4) is the permitted and supported direction. judgment.rationale: Both SFIs sit under Grade 1 (rank 1) of the same CAPS framework, but their source identity scopes differ by term and skill area: the first is Grade 1 Term 1, WRITING / Shared, Group and Independent Writing - 'Writes words using letter sounds learnt'; the second is Grade 1 Term 2, READING AND PHONICS / Daily Phonemic Awareness-Phonic Activities - 'Builds words using sounds learnt (-at, -et, -it ... at least two word families per week)'. Earlier-Term-to-later-Term direction within the same grade is permitted, and encoding words from learnt letter sounds plausibly supports success in building word families from learnt sounds, so buildsTowards first_to_second is selected over symmetric relatesTo. Shared ancestors, local rank gap of 0 and adjacent source pages are nomination signals only, not developmental evidence, so a symmetric relatesTo is the supported judgment. The Term 4 → Term 1 direction would in any case be invalid within one Grade, and the only permitted developmental direction (second_to_first) lacks pair-specific support, so a symmetric relatesTo is the best-supported judgment. judgment.rationale: Both SFIs are printed Grade R, Term 4, Emergent Reading bullets under the same Phonological/Phonemic Awareness sub-strand (same rank 0, same term, same source page/table row), so direction cannot rest on grade/term order and must come from statement content. The second SFI ('Recognises sounds at the beginning of some words') is purely auditory initial-sound awareness, tagged 'beginning sounds, phonemic awareness'. The first SFI ('Recognises aurally and visually some initial consonants and vowels especially at the beginning of common words') retains that aural task but substantively extends it: it adds the visual/letter dimension and specifies particular consonants and vowels in common words (tagged 'consonants, initial sounds, phonics, vowels'). Hearing the beginning sound of a word is the enabling capability for then matching that sound to its printed consonant or vowel, so proficiency in the second supports success in the first; this is expansion of capability, not mere repeated wording, despite the high lexical overlap flagged by the nomination. Within-grade direction stays from the narrower to the broader same-term statement, which is permitted. Both endpoints' source evidence is truncated (24 omitted evidence items each) and both carry upstream audit/merge context, so the judgment rests on the bounded excerpts and LC metadata shown.

judgment.rationale: First SFI (Grade R, Term 4, Listening and Speaking (Oral), 'Daily activities in all areas of Language and other subjects'): 'Listens to and recalls simple word sequences such as spark, bark, cart, start. Start with three words and build up to four or more' (LC tags: auditory memory, listening, recall, word sequences). Second SFI (Grade R, Term 1, same Skill Area and equivalently worded sub-strand): 'Develops skills to select and identify a specific sound when a background noise is present or music is playing, e.g. select the teacher's voice from noises or sounds in the background' (LC tags: auditory discrimination, background noise, listening, sound). These are two different auditory-perception capabilities - figure-ground sound selection versus sequential auditory memory for acoustically similar words - not the same capability at greater scope, length, complexity or independence, so the evidence does not substantiate that proficiency in one materially raises the likelihood of success in the other; the available linking signals are shared hierarchy, weak same-grade rank proximity (rank gap 0, strength 'weak') and generic LC token overlap on 'auditory'/'listening' with negligible statement-text overlap, none of which may establish developmental dependency. The pairing is nonetheless substantively coherent rather than generic repetition: both are complementary Grade R oral-language listening/auditory-perception skills taught within the same Skill Area and sub-strand, mutually reinforcing attentive listening in daily classroom activities. Canonical relatesTo with null direction and unchanged endpoint order is therefore the correct complete judgment. Confidence is moderate because both endpoints' source evidence is truncated (24 omitted source-evidence records each) and all endpoint/ancestor nodes carry upstream audit/merge context.

The differing exemplar and tag nevertheless give pair-specific instructional coherence beyond generic repetition: the same shared-reading comprehension skill is revisited later in the year through a different, complementary question type, which is meaningful reinforcement. relatesTo (symmetric, null direction, canonical endpoint order preserved) is therefore the correct judgment. judgment.rationale: Both Skills sit in Grade R, Term 1, Skill Area EMERGENT WRITING (same coordinate rank 0, same term), but under different printed sub-strands: 'Emergent Writing:' (role-plays writing in play situations - taking a telephone message, writing a traffic fine) and 'Emergent Handwriting:' (develops fine-motor control by using scissors to cut fringes). They are complementary strands of early writing development - symbolic/purposeful pretend writing versus physical fine-motor preparation for handwriting - and reinforce each other within the same term's emergent writing programme. The evidence does not show that proficiency in scissor-based fine-motor control supports success in role-playing writing purposes, or vice versa; the nomination signals are weak (shared-ancestor hierarchy, same-rank proximity, same source page 39, and only incidental token overlap on 'fine'/'etc'). Same-rank developmental direction would need substantive evidence that is absent here, so symmetric conceptual coherence within Emergent Writing is the supported judgment. Source evidence for both endpoints is truncated (24 omitted items each), so the excerpted statements are the only full statement text available.

judgment.rationale: Both SFIs are Grade 3 (rank 3, resolved coordinate) Skill statements in the Listening and Speaking (Oral) Skill Area under identically-worded 'Twice weekly focussed listening and speaking activities' sub-strands, the first with identity scope term=term 3 and the second term=term 4. The statements are near-verbatim CAPS repetitions of a single capability — listening for detail in stories and answering open-ended questions — and decompose into the same two Learning Components with the same tags (detail/listening/stories; answering/open-ended questions/speaking). The only differences are the illustrative 'e.g.' exemplar question (personal prediction 'What will you do when you grow up?' vs justified opinion 'Do you think it is right that you have to wear school uniform?') and a narrowing of named text range from 'stories and other oral texts' to 'stories'. An exemplar swap, with the one measurable scope change running backwards, is not evidence of expanded capability, greater independence, longer or more complex texts, so a developmental buildsTowards from Term 3 to Term 4 is not justified even though that direction would be permitted. The pair is nevertheless more than generic repetition: it is the same oral-comprehension skill revisited in consecutive terms of the same grade and sub-strand with complementary question types, giving useful instructional coherence without dependency, so relatesTo (symmetric, null direction, canonical endpoint order preserved) is the correct judgment. Limitations: 24 source-evidence items are omitted for each endpoint, the second endpoint's supporting LC evidence is truncated, and every endpoint and ancestor carries upstream audit/merge context (including merged Grade 3 and Term banner nodes and singleton sub-strand merge notes) that should be inspected before relying further on this evidence.
